questions.q: On a Kanban board, what does a column represent?
options: A status a piece of work passes through, like To Do, In Progress, or Done
A single developer on the team
A sprint's fixed two-week timebox
A single AWS or Azure service
questions.explain: Each column represents one status a piece of work passes through — the card moves one column to the right as the work advances.

questions.q: How many owners should a card have at any one time?
options: Exactly one — the person actually doing that piece of work right now
Zero — cards are self-managing
The entire team, collectively
Whoever most recently commented on it
questions.explain: Every card should have exactly one owner at a time. A card with no clear owner, or a blocked owner, is a signal the team needs to look at.

questions.q: Why would a team actually finish MORE work by limiting how many cards can be 'In Progress' at once (a WIP limit), rather than fewer?
options: Because starting many things at once leads to context-switching between half-finished tasks, which is slower than finishing one before starting the next
Because WIP limits are required by most project management software
Because fewer cards means less work needs to be done overall
WIP limits don't actually affect how much work gets finished
questions.explain: A developer juggling five things 'in progress' is really context-switching between five half-finished tasks. A WIP limit forces the team to finish work before pulling in more, which is what actually moves cards to Done.

questions.q: What does flagging a card as 'Blocked' communicate to the team?
options: That this card needs help from someone, not just more time
That the card should be deleted from the board
That the sprint has failed
That the card's owner is on vacation
questions.explain: Teams flag blocked cards visually so it's obvious at a glance which cards are stuck on something outside the owner's control and need intervention, versus cards that are simply still in progress.

questions.q: Which statement about Kanban-style boards and real tools is accurate?
options: Jira, Azure DevOps Boards, Trello, and GitHub Projects all implement the same column/card/WIP-limit pattern in different products
Kanban only exists inside Trello — other tools use a completely different system
Azure DevOps Boards has no connection to repos or pipelines
A team must pick exactly one of these tools and can never switch
questions.explain: Kanban is a pattern, not a single product — Jira, Azure DevOps Boards, Trello, and GitHub Projects all implement columns, cards, and WIP limits, just wired into different ecosystems (e.g. Azure DevOps Boards ties directly into Azure repos and pipelines).
